summary: Geneviève chose a life of prayer and consecrated virginity in Paris, whose patron saint she became.
A Roman soldier in Armenia, Polyeuctus died rather than offer sacrifice to pagan gods.

sourceHeading: San Severino, abate, apostolo del Norico
summary: Severinus founded monasteries in Noricum, helped poor people, and protected communities while living a life of prayer.

sourceHeading: San Severino, abate, apostolo del Norico
summary: Severinus founded monasteries in Noricum, helped poor people, and protected communities while living a life of prayer.

sourceHeading: Sant'Andrea Corsini, carmelitano, vescovo di Fiesole
summary: Andrew restored plague-damaged monasteries, helped poor people, and worked for peace as bishop of Fiesole.
Pope Agatho defended the Church’s teaching that Christ has both a divine and a human will.
Pope Agatho defended the Church’s teaching that Christ has both a divine and a human will.
Paulinus was a theologian, musician, and bishop who worked for Church reform and evangelized Slovenia.
Ancient tradition describes Hyginus as an Athenian philosopher who became pope and opposed Gnostic teaching.
Antonio served a parish in Viareggio for 48 years and encouraged lay participation in Church life.
Arcadius surrendered after a relative was arrested in his place and died rather than sacrifice to pagan gods.

sourceHeading: Sant'Ilario, vescovo di Poitiers e dottore della Chiesa
summary: Hilary became a Christian as an adult and endured exile while defending the faith as bishop of Poitiers.
Felix survived persecution, declined election as bishop, and supported himself through work while living in poverty.
Maurus was a disciple of Benedict who became abbot of Subiaco and founded a monastery in France.
John left his wealthy family for monastic life and later lived as an unrecognized beggar outside his parents’ home.
Pope Marcellus welcomed back repentant Christians who had denied their faith and died in exile.

sourceHeading: Santa Prisca, fondatrice della chiesa omonima sull'Aventino
summary: Ancient tradition honors Prisca as an early Roman martyr and associates her baptism with Saint Peter.

sourceHeading: Santi Mario, Marta, Abaco e Audiface
summary: This Christian family traveled from Persia to Rome, helped bury martyrs, and were themselves imprisoned and killed.
Germanicus, a young disciple of Polycarp, encouraged fellow Christians to remain faithful when condemned to wild beasts.
Sebastian used his military position to help imprisoned Christians before suffering martyrdom himself.
Agnes died during persecution as a young teenager because she would not abandon her Christian faith.

sourceHeading: San Vincenzo, diacono spagnolo e martire
summary: Vincent served as a deacon and preacher and endured torture before dying in Valencia in 304.

sourceHeading: San Vincenzo Pallotti, sacerdote, fondatore della Società dell’Apostolato Cattolico
summary: Vincent Pallotti taught that all baptized people, both women and men, share responsibility for proclaiming the Gospel.
Anastasius left military life, became a Christian monk, and died as a martyr in 628.
An ancient account says Emerentiana was stoned after she defended Christians gathered for Agnes’s funeral.
Ildefonsus became a monk and wrote an influential work about Mary before serving as bishop of Toledo.
Timothy Giaccardo helped lead the Pauline community in Rome and used communications media to teach the faith.

sourceHeading: Sant'Anania, che battezzò l’Apostolo Paolo in Damasco
summary: Ananias obeyed a vision directing him to Saul, laid hands on him, and helped him receive baptism.
This commemoration recalls Saul’s encounter with Christ on the road to Damascus and his transformation into the apostle Paul.
Pope Vitalian sought reconciliation with Eastern Christians and supported the Church in Britain through new episcopal appointments.

sourceHeading: San Tommaso d’Aquino, sacerdote domenicano, dottore della Chiesa, patrono delle scuole cattoliche
summary: Thomas Aquinas was a Dominican theologian who explored how reason and faith work together in the search for truth.
Perugia’s first bishop encouraged conversions during imprisonment and was eventually executed during persecution.

sourceHeading: Santi Papia e Mauro, soldati, martiri sulla via Nomentana
summary: Papias and Maurus were Roman soldiers who became Christians and suffered martyrdom during Diocletian’s persecution.
Martina distributed her wealth to poor people after becoming Christian and was later executed for her faith.
Hyacintha turned from privilege toward religious life and devoted herself to elderly and sick people.

sourceHeading: San Giovanni Bosco, sacerdote, fondatore dei Salesiani, padre e maestro dei giovani
summary: John Bosco founded the Salesians and dedicated his work to the education and spiritual care of young people.

sourceHeading: Santa Marcella, romana, discepola di San Girolamo
summary: Marcella gathered Roman women for prayer and monastic discipline under Jerome’s guidance; she died during the sack of Rome.
After becoming a widow, Ludovica joined the Franciscan Third Order and helped educate vulnerable young women.
Brigid founded a monastery at Kildare and continued the work of spreading Christianity in Ireland.

sourceHeading: Santa Caterina de' Ricci, vergine domenicana di Prato
summary: Catherine entered a Dominican monastery at fourteen and centered her contemplative life on the suffering of Jesus.

sourceHeading: San Nicola Saggio da Longobardi, laico minimo
summary: Nicholas served in humble roles among the Minims and cared for poor people in Rome.

sourceHeading: Sant' Ansgario (Oscar), vescovo di Amburgo e Brema, apostolo della Scandinavia
summary: Ansgar worked to spread Christianity in northern Europe and served as bishop of Hamburg and Bremen.
Adelaide led monasteries in Germany and adopted the Benedictine rule for her community.
Elisabeth remained devoted to her family through severe hardship and became a member of the Trinitarian Third Order.
Dorothea was a Christian from Caesarea in Cappadocia who died rather than deny her faith in Jesus.
Giovanni Maria Mastai Ferretti served as Pope Pius IX from 1846 to 1878, amid major political upheaval.

sourceHeading: San Girolamo Emiliani, fondatore dei Somaschi, patrono degli orfani e della gioventù derelitta
summary: After captivity changed his life, Jerome devoted himself to orphans and founded the community known as the Somaschi.

sourceHeading: Santi Zotico, Giacinto ed Amanzio, martiri, sulla via Labicana
summary: These martyrs suffered during Diocletian’s persecution; their relics were later moved to Rome’s Basilica of Saint Praxedes.
This day recalls Mary’s first apparition to Bernadette Soubirous at Lourdes, which became a major place of pilgrimage.
Pope Gregory II supported evangelization in northern Europe and defended the use of sacred images.
Pope Paschal I supported Scandinavian missions and moved martyrs’ relics from catacombs into Roman churches.

sourceHeading: Santi Saturnino e Compagni, martiri di Abitene in Africa
summary: These 49 Christians were arrested after Sunday worship in 304 and refused to abandon their faith under torture.

sourceHeading: Beato Giordano di Sassonia, sacerdote domenicano
summary: Jordan succeeded Dominic as leader of the Order of Preachers and worked as a missionary in Europe.

sourceHeading: San Zenone, martire sulla via Appia
summary: Zeno was an early Roman martyr whose relics Pope Paschal I placed in an oratory at Saint Praxedes.
After their conversion, Faustinus became a priest and Jovita a deacon; both died during persecution under Hadrian.
Paul welcomed Onesimus, an escaped slave, as a Christian and asked Philemon to receive him as a brother.

sourceHeading: Santa Giuliana, vergine e martire di Nicomedia, in Campania
summary: Juliana refused to abandon Christianity despite imprisonment and torture and was executed around 305.

sourceHeading: Beato Giovanni da Fiesole (Beato Angelico), sacerdote domenicano
summary: Fra Angelico was a Dominican friar whose paintings expressed his prayer and contemplation of the Christian faith.
After a destructive hunting accident, Conrad gave away his wealth and lived as a Franciscan hermit who helped sick people.
Leo opposed the destruction of sacred images and endured years away from Catania before returning as its bishop.
Maximian supported the Church in Ravenna and was associated with major church-building projects, including San Vitale.
Margaret became a Franciscan penitent and devoted herself to sick people, founding a hospital for Cortona’s poor.
Giuseppina founded the Daughters of Saint Camillus, a religious community devoted to caring for sick people.

sourceHeading: San Nestore, vescovo di Magydos e martire
summary: Nestor sheltered persecuted Christians and was killed after refusing to offer sacrifice to idols.
Tradition remembers Faustiniano as Bologna’s second bishop, whose preaching strengthened Christians during persecution.
Gabriel left a worldly life to become a Passionist and died at only twenty-four in 1862.
Romanus lived as a hermit in the Jura and founded a monastic community at Condat with his brother Lupicinus.
Pope Felix III defended Church teaching and supported African bishops during the Vandal invasions.
Humbert governed Savoy while maintaining a strong desire for monastic life and supporting the abbey of Hautecombe.
John Joseph embraced Franciscan poverty and helped reunite the Alcantarine Franciscan community in which he served.

sourceHeading: Santa Rosa da Viterbo, vergine francescana
summary: Rose was a young Franciscan tertiary who preached in Viterbo and died at eighteen in 1251.

sourceHeading: Santa Coletta Boylet, vergine francescana, fondatrice delle Clarisse povere
summary: Colette reformed communities of Poor Clares, emphasizing poverty, discipline, and the prayer of the Church.
Perpetua and Felicity were African Christians arrested in 203 who suffered martyrdom under Emperor Septimius Severus.

sourceHeading: Santa Teresa Margherita Redi, vergine carmelitana
summary: Teresa Margaret combined Carmelite contemplation with care for sick sisters in her Florence community.

sourceHeading: San Giovanni di Dio, fondatore dei Fatebenefratelli, patrono degli Infermi e Ospedalieri
summary: After a life of travel and hardship, John of God recognized his calling to care for sick people in Granada.
Forty Christian soldiers at Sebaste accepted death from winter exposure rather than abandon their faith.
Catherine left court life for the Poor Clares and later founded and led a monastery in Bologna.

sourceHeading: Santa Francesca romana, fondatrice delle Oblate di Tor de’ Specchi
summary: Frances of Rome used her wealth and social position to serve people living in poverty.
Pope Simplicius guided the Church during the collapse of the Western Roman Empire and defended its teaching about Christ.

sourceHeading: San Giovanni Ogilvie, sacerdote gesuita e martire
summary: John Ogilvie secretly ministered to Catholics in Scotland and was executed in Glasgow in 1615.
Sophronius defended Christian teaching as bishop of Jerusalem and secured freedom of worship during the city’s conquest.
Eulogius was a priest of Córdoba who openly defended Christianity and suffered martyrdom in 859.
Maximilian refused military service because of his Christian convictions and was executed at Tebessa in 295.
Pope Innocent I led the Church during the Visigoth siege of Rome and opposed the teaching of Pelagius.
Sabinus hid with other persecuted Christians in Egypt before being arrested and killed in 303.
Little is known of Christina, a Persian convert to Christianity who died for her faith in 559.
Leander helped bring the Visigothic royal family from Arianism into Catholic communion and served as bishop of Seville.
Matilda became queen of Germany but placed her desire for holiness above royal wealth and status.

sourceHeading: Beato Placido Riccardi, monaco di San Paolo fuori le mura
summary: Placido was a Benedictine priest who worked to restore Farfa Abbey and faithfully observed the monastic rule.

sourceHeading: San Clemente M. Hofbauer, presbitero redentorista
summary: Clement Hofbauer served as a Redemptorist priest, helping poor people and promoting Church renewal in Austria.
Pope Zachary worked as a mediator during conflicts involving the Eastern Empire and the Lombards.

sourceHeading: Santi Ilario e Taziano, martiri di Aquileia
summary: Hilarius was a bishop and Tatianus a deacon whose martyrdom is commemorated at Aquileia and Gorizia.

sourceHeading: San Giovanni Sarcander, sacerdote e martire
summary: John Sarkander was imprisoned amid religious conflict and died as a martyr in 1620.

sourceHeading: San Cirillo, vescovo di Gerusalemme e dottore della Chiesa
summary: Cyril endured repeated exile while defending the faith and became known for his instruction of people preparing for baptism.
Anselm of Lucca promoted spiritual renewal and maintained a strong commitment to monastic life.

sourceHeading: San Giovanni Nepomuceno, sacerdote e martire di Praga
summary: John Nepomucene opposed royal interference in the Church and is remembered for defending the sacredness of confession.

sourceHeading: San Nicola di Flüe, patrono della Svizzera
summary: Nicholas became a hermit after raising a family and continued to work for peace in Switzerland.

sourceHeading: San Paolo, vescovo di Narbonne e martire
summary: Paul traveled to Gaul to preach and became the first bishop of the Christian community at Narbonne.
Leah, a Roman widow, chose community life and ascetic discipline instead of remarriage and helped guide younger women.

sourceHeading: San Turibio de Mogrovejo, vescovo di Lima
summary: Turibius served as bishop of Lima, working to evangelize Indigenous communities and improve the conduct of the clergy.

sourceHeading: Santa Caterina di Svezia, vergine, figlia di Santa Brigida
summary: Catherine, daughter of Bridget of Sweden, lived a life of prayer and became the first abbess of Vadstena.

sourceHeading: San Quirino, martire sulla via Portuense
summary: Tradition describes Quirinus as a Roman officer converted through contact with Christian prisoners who later suffered martyrdom himself.

sourceHeading: Santa Lucia Filippini, fondatrice delle Maestre Pie Filippini
summary: Lucy Filippini promoted education and religious instruction for poor girls and founded the Maestre Pie Filippini.

sourceHeading: San Giovanni Climaco, abate del Sinai
summary: John Climacus lived as a monk and hermit at Sinai and wrote the spiritual work known as The Ladder.
Amadeus and his wife Yolande combined their responsibilities as rulers with faith and generous care for poor people.
Benjamin was a deacon who died for refusing to worship idols and remaining faithful to the Gospel.
Sixtus I led the early Roman Church and was buried near Saint Peter after his death.

sourceHeading: Sant'Isidoro, vescovo di Siviglia e dottore della Chiesa
summary: Isidore of Seville gathered the learning of his time into writings that became important resources throughout medieval Europe.
Vincent Ferrer was a Dominican preacher who worked for Church unity during the Western Schism.
After becoming a widow, Galla devoted herself to fasting and charity before retiring to a monastery.

sourceHeading: San Giovanni Battista de la Salle, sacerdote, fondatore dei Fratelli delle Scuole Cristiane
summary: John Baptist de La Salle founded the Brothers of the Christian Schools and made the education of young people his life's work.

sourceHeading: Santa Maddalena di Canossa, vergine, fondatrice dei Figli e delle Figlie di Carità
summary: Magdalene of Canossa founded the Daughters of Charity. She taught a simple, joyful way of serving God and others.

sourceHeading: Santo Stanislao, vescovo di Cracovia e martire
summary: Stanislaus, Bishop of Krakow, cared for poor people and challenged King Boleslaus II. He was killed in 1079.

sourceHeading: Santa Gemma Galgani, vergine lucchese, terziaria passionista
summary: Gemma Galgani remained devoted to Christ through illness and family loss. The young lay mystic died in 1903.
Pope Julius I defended the Church's teaching on the Trinity during the Arian dispute and supported councils at Rome and Sardica.
Zeno came from North Africa and became Bishop of Verona. He was known for humility and care for poor people.

sourceHeading: San Giuseppe Moscati, medico di Napoli
summary: Giuseppe Moscati was a doctor in Naples. He treated people in need with special care and died in 1927.

sourceHeading: San Martino I, papa e martire
summary: Pope Martin I defended the faith against Monothelitism. He was imprisoned and exiled to Crimea, where he died in 655.
Hermenegild was a Visigothic prince who became Catholic. He was imprisoned and killed after refusing communion from an Arian bishop.

sourceHeading: Santi Tiburzio, Valeriano e Massimo, martiri, sulla via Appia
summary: Cecilia brought her husband Valerian to faith. Valerian, his brother Tiburtius, and their converted jailer Maximus suffered martyrdom.
Abundius served humbly at Saint Peter's in Rome. Gregory the Great recalled his faith and a healing associated with him.
Bernadette Soubirous was a poor girl from Lourdes. Her account of Mary's appearances called people to prayer and conversion.
Leo IX worked for Church reform and opposed the sale of Church offices. His papacy also faced the division between East and West.
Apollonius defended Christianity before the Roman Senate. His account presented faith through philosophical reasoning before his martyrdom.

sourceHeading: Sant'Anselmo, arcivescovo di Canterbury e dottore della Chiesa
summary: Anselm was a Benedictine monk, theologian, and Archbishop of Canterbury. His work joined faith with careful study and pastoral service.
Pope Agapetus I travelled to Constantinople on a mission of peace. He defended the faith and died there in 536.

sourceHeading: Beata Maria Gabriella Sagheddu, vergine cistercense
summary: Maria Gabriella Sagheddu was a Sardinian Cistercian nun. She offered her life for Christian unity and died of tuberculosis at twenty-five.

sourceHeading: San Fedele da Sigmaringen, sacerdote, martire
summary: Fidelis of Sigmaringen left legal work to become a Capuchin. He preached in Switzerland and was killed in 1622.

sourceHeading: Beata Maria Elisabeth Hesselblad, fondatrice delle Brigidine
summary: Elizabeth Hesselblad became Catholic after a Lutheran upbringing. She renewed Bridgettine religious life and worked for Christian unity.
Mark accompanied Paul and Peter. Christian tradition connects his Gospel with Peter's teaching about Jesus.

sourceHeading: San Simeone, vescovo di Gerusalemme e martire
summary: Simeon led the Christian community in Jerusalem after James. Tradition remembers his crucifixion during the reign of Trajan.

sourceHeading: San Pietro Chanel, sacerdote e martire dell'Oceania
summary: Peter Chanel was a Marist priest sent to Futuna. His missionary service ended in martyrdom in 1841.

sourceHeading: San Luigi Maria Grignion de Montfort, sacerdote fondatore della Compagnia di Maria
summary: Louis de Montfort preached devotion to Mary and the Cross. He founded religious communities and wrote True Devotion to Mary.

sourceHeading: Santa Caterina da Siena, vergine, dottore della Chiesa, Patrona d’Europa e d’Italia
summary: Catherine of Siena worked for peace and unity in the Church. She urged the pope to return from Avignon to Rome.
Pope Pius V cared for people in need. He established a feast connected with the Rosary after the battle of Lepanto.
Peter the Deacon was a Benedictine who assisted Gregory the Great. He served in Sicily, Campania, and Rome.
Jeremiah called Judah to return to God. His warnings about Jerusalem brought persecution and imprisonment.

sourceHeading: Sant'Atanasio, vescovo di Alessandria d'Egitto e dottore della Chiesa
summary: Athanasius, Bishop of Alexandria, defended the divinity of Christ during the Arian dispute. His witness shaped the Church's teaching.

sourceHeading: Santi Filippo e Giacomo il Minore, apostoli
summary: Philip and James were among the Twelve Apostles. Their relics are honoured together at the Basilica of the Holy Apostles in Rome.

sourceHeading: Santi Evenzio, Alessandro e Teodulo, martiri sulla via Nomentana
summary: These Roman martyrs were buried along the Via Nomentana. The Italian Vatican account distinguishes this Alexander from Pope Alexander I.
Antonina suffered imprisonment during the persecution under Diocletian. She remained faithful to Christ through martyrdom at Nicaea.

sourceHeading: S. Nunzio Sulprizio, giovane operaio di Napoli
summary: Nunzio Sulprizio endured harsh treatment as a young worker and suffered serious illness. He died at nineteen in 1836.
Marian and James encouraged Christians in Numidia to remain faithful. They suffered martyrdom during the persecution of 259.
Flavia Domitilla was a Christian woman of noble Roman birth. She endured exile on the island of Ponza for her faith.

sourceHeading: Santa Rosa Venerini, vergine, fondatrice delle Maestre Pie Venerini
summary: Rosa Venerini saw a need for education while praying with women. She founded a teaching community to help girls learn.
Victor was a soldier from North Africa. He refused to abandon his Christian faith and suffered martyrdom in Milan.
Pope Boniface IV dedicated the Pantheon in Rome to Mary and the martyrs. He had been a Benedictine monk.
Pope Benedict II worked to simplify the confirmation of papal elections. His short pontificate ended with his death in 685.

sourceHeading: Sant'Arsenio, diacono domano, anacoreta in Egitto
summary: Arsenius left service in Rome for the Egyptian desert. He devoted his later life to silence, prayer, and contemplation.
Isaiah was one of Israel's great prophets. His preaching called the people to faithfulness, and tradition remembers him as a martyr.
Pachomius first encountered Christian kindness while imprisoned. He later became a leader of monks and helped shape community monastic life.

sourceHeading: Santa Luisa de Marillac, cofondatrice delle Figlie della Carità
summary: Louise de Marillac was a widow who devoted herself to charity. With Vincent de Paul, she founded the Daughters of Charity.

sourceHeading: San Giordano, martire sulla via Latina
summary: Gordian was converted through a priest he had persecuted. He later suffered martyrdom and was buried along Rome's Via Latina.
John of Avila was a Spanish priest and preacher who guided many people in faith. He was declared a Doctor of the Church.

sourceHeading: Santi Quarto e Quinti, martiri di Roma
summary: Quartus and Quintus are remembered as Roman martyrs associated with the Via Latina. Few details of their lives are known.
Anthimus brought others to Christianity, including a pagan priest. After his arrest, he suffered martyrdom near the Via Salaria.

sourceHeading: Santi Nereo e Achilleo, martiri sulla via Ardeatina
summary: Nereus and Achilleus were Roman martyrs. Their burial place in the Catacombs of Domitilla became a place of Christian remembrance.

sourceHeading: San Pancrazio, martire sulla via Aurelia
summary: Pancras was a young convert to Christianity in Rome. He was executed for his faith during the persecution of 304.
Germanus, Patriarch of Constantinople, defended sacred images and the Church's teaching. He died in the eighth century.
At Fatima in 1917, three children reported appearances of Mary. The message called people to prayer, penance, and conversion.
Matthias was chosen by lot to take Judas's place among the Apostles. The Acts of the Apostles records his selection.

sourceHeading: San Michele Garicoïts, sacerdote, fondatore dei Preti del s. Cuore di Gesù di Bétharram
summary: Michael Garicoits founded the Priests of the Sacred Heart of Betharram. He worked to renew faith among clergy, young people, and rural communities.
Torquatus is honoured as the first Bishop of Guadix. Tradition places him among the early bishops who brought Christianity to Spain.
Isidore worked as a farmer near Madrid. With his wife Maria, he joined daily work and prayer with generosity to poor people.

sourceHeading: Sant'Alessandro, vescovo di Gerusalemme e martire
summary: Alexander, Bishop of Jerusalem, supported Christian learning and established a library. He died in prison during persecution in 250.
Ubald served as Bishop of Gubbio for thirty-one years. He sought peace and protected his community during conflict.

sourceHeading: San Vittore, martire sulla via Salaria antica
summary: Victor is remembered as a Roman martyr buried in the cemetery of Basilla on the Via Salaria. Little else is known.

sourceHeading: San Pasquale Baylon, laico francescano, patrono delle Associazioni eucaristiche
summary: Paschal Baylon worked as a shepherd before joining the Franciscans. He became known for his deep devotion to the Eucharist.

sourceHeading: San Giovanni I, papa e martire
summary: Pope John I travelled to Constantinople on an embassy. King Theodoric later imprisoned him at Ravenna, where he died in 526.

sourceHeading: San Felice da Cantalice, religioso cappuccino
summary: Felix of Cantalice was a Capuchin who collected alms in Rome for forty years. His service joined prayer with practical charity.

sourceHeading: San Pietro Celestino V, papa (Pietro da Morrone)
summary: The hermit Peter of Morrone became Pope Celestine V in 1294. He established the Perdonanza pardon and later resigned the papacy.
Urban I led the Church in Rome during the third century. Few reliable details of his life and death survive.
Parthenius and Calogerus are remembered as martyrs of the persecution of 304. They were buried in the cemetery of Callistus.
Ives was a priest and lawyer in Brittany. He provided legal help without payment and welcomed people in need.

sourceHeading: San Crispino da Viterbo, religioso cappuccino
summary: Crispin of Viterbo served as a Capuchin gardener and alms collector. People sought his practical wisdom during his long service at Orvieto.

sourceHeading: San Bernardino da Siena, sacerdote francescano
summary: Bernardine of Siena was a Franciscan preacher. His clear teaching reached many people, and he worked for renewal within his order.
Aurea is honoured as a martyr of Ostia. She remained faithful to Christ when ordered to abandon her faith.

sourceHeading: Santi Cristoforo Magallanes, sacerdote, e Compagni, martiri in Messico
summary: Christopher Magallanes and his companions remained faithful during religious persecution in Mexico. They were canonized together in 2000.

sourceHeading: Sant'Eugenio de Mazenod, vescovo di Marsiglia, fondatore degli Oblati di Maria Immacolata
summary: Eugene de Mazenod founded the Missionary Oblates of Mary Immaculate. As Bishop of Marseille, he continued his work of preaching and service.

sourceHeading: San Giovanni Battista de Rossi, sacerdote romano
summary: John Baptist de Rossi was a priest in Rome. He became known as a confessor and a guide for people seeking spiritual help.
Vincent of Lerins was a monk who wrote the Commonitorium. His work offered guidance on keeping the Church's received faith.
Pope Gregory VII worked for Church reform. His conflict with Henry IV concerned the appointment of bishops and led to the meeting at Canossa.

sourceHeading: San Beda Venerabile, sacerdote benedettino, dottore della Chiesa
summary: Bede was an English monk, historian, and student of Scripture. He devoted his life to prayer, teaching, and writing.
Mary Magdalene de Pazzi was a Carmelite in Florence. Her prayer and spiritual life included a strong concern for reform in the Church.
Eleutherius served as Bishop of Rome in the second century. His pontificate faced disputes about Christian teaching.
Augustine was a Benedictine sent to preach in England. He became Archbishop of Canterbury and died in 604.
Germain served as Bishop of Paris and helped restore monastic life. His ministry showed particular care for his community.

sourceHeading: Santa Ursula Ledóchowska, fondatrice delle Orsoline del s. Cuore di Gesù agonizzante
summary: Ursula Ledochowska worked as an educator in several countries. She founded a congregation and served poor, elderly, and sick people.
Pope Paul VI completed the Second Vatican Council and guided its reforms. His journeys took his ministry to five continents.
Ferdinand united the kingdoms of Castile and Leon. He supported religious and educational works, including Burgos Cathedral and the University of Salamanca.
Joan of Arc led French forces at Orleans. She was later condemned for heresy and burned at the stake in 1431.
Pope Eugene I defended the Church's teaching during disputes with Constantinople. His pontificate lasted from 654 to 657.

sourceHeading: Santi Carlo Lwanga e Compagni, martiri dell’Uganda
summary: Charles Lwanga and his companions were Christian martyrs in nineteenth-century Uganda. Their witness is especially remembered at Namugongo.
Clotilda, Queen of the Franks, raised her children in the Christian faith. She later devoted herself to prayer and charity at Tours.

sourceHeading: San Francesco Caracciolo, sacerdote, fondatore dei Chierici Regolari Minori
summary: Francis Caracciolo helped found the Clerics Regular Minor. Devotion to Mary and Eucharistic adoration marked his religious life.

sourceHeading: San Norberto, vescovo di Magdeburgo, fondatore dei Canonici Regolari Premostratensi
summary: Norbert travelled as a preacher and worked for peace. He founded the Premonstratensians and later became Archbishop of Magdeburg.

sourceHeading: Santi Artemio e Paolina, martiri sulla via Aurelia
summary: Artemius and Paulina became Christians after their daughter's healing through Peter and Marcellinus. Their family suffered martyrdom for the faith.

sourceHeading: San Claudio di Condat, abate e vescovo
summary: Claudius served as Bishop of Besancon and as abbot of Condat. He is remembered for his monastic and pastoral service.

sourceHeading: Sant'Antonio Maria Gianelli, vescovo di Bobbio, fondatore delle Figlie di Maria
summary: Anthony Mary Gianelli was born in Liguria in 1789. He became a priest and later served as Bishop of Bobbio.

sourceHeading: Beata Anna Maria Taigi, madre di famiglia
summary: Anna Maria Taigi was a mother of seven and a Trinitarian tertiary. She served poor and sick people while caring for her family.
Primus and Felician were brothers who suffered martyrdom. Their relics were later brought to the church of Santo Stefano Rotondo in Rome.
Landry, Bishop of Paris, sold possessions to feed people in need. He also helped establish hospital care for the community.
Barnabas was an early Christian missionary. He encouraged Paul and helped the Church welcome people beyond its first communities.

sourceHeading: San Restituto, martire sulla via Nomentana
summary: Restitutus refused to offer a pagan sacrifice. He suffered martyrdom in Rome and was buried along the Via Nomentana.
John of Sahagun gave up wealth and became an Augustinian. He joined prayer and Eucharistic devotion with care for poor people in Salamanca.
Onuphrius left community monastic life for the desert. Tradition, associated with Paphnutius, remembers his long life of solitude and prayer.
Pope Leo III defended the Church's teaching about Christ. He crowned Charlemagne as emperor in Rome in 800.
Elisha succeeded Elijah as a prophet of Israel. Scripture recalls his preaching and the wonders associated with his ministry.

sourceHeading: San Bernardo da Mentone, canonico regolare di Sant'Agostino
summary: Bernard of Menthon provided hospitality for travellers in the Alps. His preaching and mountain foundations served people on difficult journeys.
Germaine Cousin lived with disability and rejection within her family. While tending sheep, she maintained a life of prayer and trust in God.
Quiricus and his mother Julitta are honoured as martyrs of Tarsus. Their witness is remembered together in the Church's calendar.

sourceHeading: Santi Biagio e Diogene, martiri sulla via Salaria antica
summary: Blaise and Diogenes are early martyrs whose relics are honoured at Saint Praxedes in Rome. Few details of their lives survive.

sourceHeading: San Gregorio Barbarigo, vescovo di Padova e cardinale
summary: Gregory Barbarigo cared for plague victims and people in poverty. As a bishop, he also gave close attention to the formation of priests.
Marina lived in a monastery with her father, disguised as a boy. Tradition remembers her patience when she faced false accusations.

sourceHeading: Ss. Gervaso e Protaso, martiri milanesi
summary: Gervasius and Protasius were martyrs whose remains Ambrose found in 386. They are honoured at his basilica in Milan.
Romuald joined monastic life with a strong call to solitude. He founded Camaldoli and helped renew the Benedictine tradition.

sourceHeading: San Luigi Gonzaga, gesuita, patrono della gioventù cattolica
summary: Aloysius Gonzaga gave up his inheritance to become a Jesuit. He served plague victims and died during the epidemic of 1591.

sourceHeading: San Giovanni Fisher, vescovo di Rochester, martire inglese
summary: John Fisher, Bishop of Rochester, refused to recognize Henry VIII as head of the Church. He was executed in 1535.

sourceHeading: San Flavio Clemente, console romano, martire
summary: Flavius Clemens was a Roman consul remembered for his Christian faith. He suffered martyrdom during the reign of Domitian.
Innocent V was a Dominican theologian and former Archbishop of Lyon. His short papacy in 1276 continued efforts toward Christian unity.
Thomas More defended the claims of conscience against political power. He was executed in 1535 after refusing Henry VIII's authority over the Church.
John the Baptist prepared the way for Jesus. The Church celebrates both his birth, on June 24, and his martyrdom.

sourceHeading: Santi Giovanni e Festo, martiri sulla via Salaria antica
summary: John and Festus are Roman martyrs remembered together. Their burial place was along the old Via Salaria, but little is known about their lives.
Prosper of Aquitaine was a lay monk and theologian. He defended Augustine's teaching and wrote about God's saving grace.
John and Paul are remembered as brothers in faith and family. Tradition places their martyrdom and burial at their home on Rome's Caelian Hill.

sourceHeading: San Josemaria Escrivá de Balaguer, sacerdote, fondatore dell’Opus Dei
summary: Josemaria Escriva founded Opus Dei. His teaching encouraged people from every walk of life to seek holiness.

sourceHeading: San Cirillo d'Alessandria, vescovo e dottore della Chiesa
summary: Cyril of Alexandria defended faith in Jesus Christ, the incarnate Word of God. Both Eastern and Western Christians honour him.
The first Roman martyrs were Christians falsely blamed by Nero for the fire of Rome in 64. They suffered torture and death.

sourceHeading: Santi Giulio e Aronne, martiri di Bretagna
summary: Julius and Aaron are honoured as early Christian martyrs in Britain. Their memory is especially associated with Caerleon.

sourceHeading: Santi Processo e Martiniano, martiri romani
summary: Tradition remembers Processus and Martinian as guards converted by Peter and Paul during their imprisonment. They later suffered martyrdom for their faith.
Elizabeth of Portugal cared for poor people and worked for peace between rulers. After her husband's death, she entered religious life at Coimbra.
Ulrich served as Bishop of Augsburg for fifty years. He defended his people, supported the clergy, and cared for the city.

sourceHeading: Beata Maria Teresa Ledóchowska, fondatrice delle Suore missionarie di S. Pietro Claver
summary: Mary Theresa Ledochowska came from a Polish family in Austria. Encounters with missionaries led her to support African missions and oppose slavery.
The Dominican Nicholas Boccasini became Pope Benedict XI in 1303. He had worked for peace between France and England.
Eugene III became a Cistercian after meeting Bernard of Clairvaux. As pope, he retained monastic simplicity and worked for Church reform.
Adrian III was pope from 884 to 885. He sought good relations with Constantinople and died while travelling north from Rome.

sourceHeading: Santa Veronica Giuliani, abbadessa, clarissa cappuccina
summary: Veronica Giuliani spent fifty years as a Poor Clare at Citta di Castello. Her mystical life centred on Christ's suffering.
Anatolia and Victoria were young Roman women who refused marriage after dedicating themselves to God. Tradition remembers their imprisonment and martyrdom in Sabina.
Pius I led the Church in Rome in the second century. His pontificate faced Marcion's teaching about God and the Scriptures.

sourceHeading: San Giovanni Gualberto, abate, fondatore dei Vallombrosani
summary: John Gualbert opposed the sale of Church offices and founded Vallombrosa. His monastic community emphasized poverty, work, and the example of the Apostles.

sourceHeading: Santi Nabore e Felice, martiri milanesi
summary: Nabor and Felix were soldiers from North Africa who became Christians. They suffered martyrdom at Lodi and were later honoured in Milan.

sourceHeading: San Camillo de Lellis, sacerdote, fondatore dei Ministri degli Infermi
summary: Camillus de Lellis devoted his life to caring for sick people. Benedict XVI presented him as an outstanding example of practical Christian charity.

sourceHeading: San Bonaventura da Bagnoregio, cardinale, vescovo di Albano e dottore della Chiesa, francescano
summary: Bonaventure was a Franciscan theologian and Doctor of the Church. He helped shape Franciscan thought and died during the Council of Lyon in 1274.
Pompilio Maria Pirotti joined the Piarists to educate poor young people. His tireless work in central Italy earned him lasting affection.

sourceHeading: Santa Maria Maddalena Postel, vergine, fondatrice delle Suore delle Scuole Cristiane della Misericordia
summary: Mary Magdalene Postel taught girls and instructed children in the faith. After the French Revolution, she founded the Daughters of Mercy.

sourceHeading: Santa Marcellina, vergine, sorella di Sant'Ambrogio, vescovo
summary: Marcellina was the sister of Ambrose and Satyrus. She lived a consecrated life of prayer, supported Ambrose, and cared for poor people.
Pope Leo IV guided Rome through military threats and natural disasters. His eight-year pontificate combined pastoral care with efforts to protect the city.
Bruno, Bishop of Segni, defended belief in Christ's presence in the Eucharist. He opposed abuses before retiring to monastic life at Montecassino.
Emilian openly opposed the restoration of pagan worship at Durostorum. He was condemned to death during the reign of Julian.

sourceHeading: Sant'Apollinare, vescovo di Ravenna a martire
summary: Apollinaris is honoured as the first Bishop of Ravenna. Tradition remembers his long work of preaching in the region and his martyrdom.
Elijah called the people of Israel to worship the Lord alone. His prophetic ministry challenged idolatry and demanded faithfulness to God.

sourceHeading: Santa Prassede, romana,nella chiesa da lei fondata sull'Esquilino
summary: Praxedes belonged to a Christian household in Rome. Tradition remembers her support for Christian worship and her witness during persecution.
Ezekiel encouraged the people of Israel during exile in Babylon. His prophetic book uses vivid visions and symbols to proclaim God's word.
Bridget of Sweden was a wife, mother of eight, and founder of a religious order. She urged the pope to return to Rome.
Charbel Makhlouf was a Maronite monk who became a hermit in Lebanon. Silence and prayer shaped his life, and many healings are attributed to his intercession.
James the Greater was one of Jesus's Apostles. The pilgrimage to his shrine at Santiago de Compostela has drawn Christians for centuries.

sourceHeading: Santi Gioacchino e Anna, genitori della Beata Vergine Maria
summary: Joachim and Anne are remembered as Mary's parents and Jesus's grandparents. Their names come from ancient Christian tradition rather than Scripture.
Pope Celestine I served from 422 to 432. He supported churches in Rome and defended the faith against Pelagian and Nestorian teaching.
Simeon the Stylite lived mainly in Syria. His unusual life of prayer on a pillar made him a widely known witness to ascetic devotion.
Pantaleon was a physician at Nicomedia who treated poor people without payment. He suffered martyrdom after being denounced to the authorities.
Pope Urban II opposed the sale of Church offices and clerical corruption. He called the First Crusade and died in Rome in 1099.

sourceHeading: Santi Nazario e Celso, martiri milanesi
summary: Tradition remembers Nazarius as a preacher who baptized the young Celsus. They became companions in Christian witness and suffered martyrdom in Milan.
Pope Victor I came from Africa. He opposed teachings that denied Christ's divine sonship and worked for a common observance of Easter.
Martha, Mary, and Lazarus welcomed Jesus as friend and Lord. Martha's service expressed a faith rooted in love and trust in him.
Abdon and Sennen were Persian Christians who helped bury martyrs in Rome. They refused pagan sacrifice and suffered martyrdom themselves.

sourceHeading: San Giustino de Jacobis, della Congregazione della Missione, vescovo in Abissinia
summary: Justin de Jacobis served the Church in Ethiopia. He trained local clergy and worked for Christian unity with respect for local traditions.

sourceHeading: Sant'Alfonso Maria de’ Liguori, vescovo e dottore della Chiesa, fondatore della Congregazione del Ss.mo Redentore
summary: Alphonsus Liguori left a legal career to become a priest. He founded the Redemptorists and later served as Bishop of Sant'Agata dei Goti.
The seven Maccabean brothers and their mother died rather than abandon God's law. The Church remembers them as forerunners of Christian martyrs.
Eusebius, the first Bishop of Vercelli, defended the Nicene faith. After years of exile, he returned to continue his pastoral work.
Pope Stephen I welcomed the return of Christians who had fallen away. He opposed repeating baptism for those returning from heresy.

sourceHeading: Santa Lidia, discepola di San Paolo
summary: Lydia sold purple cloth in Philippi. After her household received baptism, she welcomed Paul and provided a home for the Christian community.

sourceHeading: San Giovanni M. Vianney, curato d’Ars, patrono del clero con cura d’anime
summary: John Vianney served as parish priest of Ars. He gave long hours to hearing confessions and helping people return to God.
Justin and Crescentius were Roman Christians associated with the Via Tiburtina. Tradition remembers Justin's charity in burying martyrs.
Pope Hormisdas was a widowed deacon before his election. His profession of faith helped restore communion between Rome and Constantinople.

sourceHeading: Santi Sisto II, papa, e compagni, martiri
summary: Pope Sixtus II sought peace within the Church. He and his companions were killed during Valerian's persecution in 258.

sourceHeading: San Gaetano Thiene, sacerdote, fondatore dei Teatini
summary: Cajetan cared for poor and seriously ill people. With companions, he founded the Theatines to renew priestly life through the Gospel.
Donatus fled persecution and settled at Arezzo. He preached and prayed there before becoming its bishop and suffering martyrdom.
Albert of Trapani was a Carmelite known for prayer and preaching. He served as provincial in Sicily until his death in 1307.

sourceHeading: Santi Ciriaco, Largo e Smaragdo, martiri
summary: Cyriacus, Largus, and Smaragdus helped Christians forced to build Diocletian's baths. They were imprisoned and suffered martyrdom for their service and faith.

sourceHeading: San Romano, martire sulla via Tiburtina
summary: Romanus was a soldier moved by Lawrence's suffering. He asked Lawrence for baptism and was killed after declaring himself a Christian.

sourceHeading: San Tiburzio, martire sulla via Labicana
summary: Tiburtius was an early Roman martyr praised by Pope Damasus. His tomb on the Via Labicana drew pilgrims in later centuries.
Susanna dedicated herself to Christ and refused a proposed marriage. Tradition places her martyrdom at the Roman house that became her church.

sourceHeading: Santa Giovanna Francesca di Chantal, religiosa
summary: Jane Frances de Chantal served poor people while raising her family. After becoming a widow, she founded the Visitation community with Francis de Sales.
Pope Innocent XI opposed abuses, nepotism, and slavery. His pontificate also faced the siege of Vienna and conflict with Ottoman forces.

sourceHeading: Ss. Ponziano, papa e Ippolito, sacerdote, martiri
summary: Pope Pontian resigned after exile to the mines of Sardinia. He and Hippolytus died there and are honoured as martyrs.
Cassian of Imola taught young people and shared his Christian faith. He suffered martyrdom after refusing to sacrifice to idols.
John Berchmans worked to support his studies before joining the Jesuits. He died in Rome at twenty-two while preparing for priesthood.

sourceHeading: Sant'Eusebio, romano, fondatore della chiesa omonima sull'Esquilino
summary: Eusebius was a Roman priest remembered for opposing Arian influence. Tradition connects his imprisonment and death with his defence of the faith.
Tarcisius died while protecting the Eucharist he was carrying to others. The Church honours him as a patron of altar servers.
Stephen, King of Hungary, helped establish dioceses and abbeys. His rule supported the growth and organization of the Church in his country.
Roch gave away his possessions and became a pilgrim. During his journey, he cared for people suffering from plague.
Pope Eusebius sought to guide Christians returning after denying the faith during persecution. Conflict over their reconciliation led to his exile.

sourceHeading: San Giacinto di Cracovia, sacerdote domenicano
summary: Hyacinth joined the Dominicans after meeting Dominic in Rome. He preached in Poland and farther east and worked for unity between Christians.

sourceHeading: Santa Chiara da Montefalco, abbadessa agostiniana
summary: Clare of Montefalco entered religious life as a child and later became an abbess. Her prayer centred on Christ's Passion.
Agapitus was a young Christian from Palestrina. Tradition remembers his martyrdom at fifteen after he refused to deny his faith.

sourceHeading: San Giovanni Eudes, sacerdote, fondatore degli Eudisti
summary: John Eudes cared for plague victims and preached among people suffering from war. He founded the Congregation of Jesus and Mary.
Pope Sixtus III supported reconciliation between Antioch and Alexandria. His pontificate is also associated with Rome's Basilica of Saint Mary Major.
Tradition places Magnus among the soldiers who refused to kill Christians. He continued to spread the faith before suffering martyrdom.
Samuel was a prophet and judge of Israel. Scripture tells how God called him and sent him to anoint Saul and David.

sourceHeading: Santa Maria de Mattias, fondatrice delle Adoratrici del Preziosissimo Sangue
summary: Mary de Mattias preached throughout the countryside of central Italy. She founded the Adorers of the Blood of Christ, with a mission of education.
Pope Pius X served from 1903 to 1914. He is widely remembered for the catechism associated with his name.

sourceHeading: San Timoteo, martire romano sulla via Ostiense
summary: Timothy was a Roman martyr associated with the Via Ostiense. Tradition remembers his preaching, though few historical details survive.
Symphorian was raised as a Christian in Autun. He openly professed his faith during a pagan procession and was condemned to death.

sourceHeading: San Filippo Benizi, sacerdote dei Servi di Maria
summary: Philip Benizi joined the Servants of Mary and first performed humble tasks. He later became a priest and led the order's growth.

sourceHeading: Santa Rosa da Lima, vergine, terziaria domenicana
summary: Rose of Lima devoted her short life to Christ in prayer and sacrifice. She became the first canonized saint of the Americas.

sourceHeading: Santi Abbondio e Ireneo, martiri sulla via Tiburtina
summary: Abundius and Irenaeus buried the martyr Concordia with care. They were killed during persecution and buried along Rome's Via Tiburtina.
Bartholomew was one of the Twelve Apostles. Christian tradition remembers his later preaching and his martyrdom in Armenia.

sourceHeading: Santa Giovanna Antida Thouret, vergine, fondatrice delle Suore di Carità
summary: Jeanne Antide Thouret came from a poor French family. She founded the Sisters of Charity and continued her work despite many difficulties.
Emily de Vialar founded the Sisters of Saint Joseph of the Apparition in France. Her congregation took up a missionary vocation.

sourceHeading: San Giuseppe Calasanzio, sacerdote, fondatore degli Scolopi
summary: Joseph Calasanz saw the needs of poor children in Rome. He devoted his life to free education and founded the Piarists.
Pope Zephyrinus defended the Church's teaching about the Father and the Son. He entrusted Callistus with the Christian cemetery on the Via Appia.

sourceHeading: San Massimiliano, martire sulla via Salaria antica
summary: Little is known about the Roman martyr Maximilian. By the seventh century, pilgrims were visiting his tomb near the old Via Salaria.
Tradition remembers Alexander as a soldier who refused orders against Christians. He suffered martyrdom at Bergamo and became its patron.
Pammachius was a Christian Roman senator who devoted himself to poor people. He helped provide free shelter for sick and needy pilgrims.

sourceHeading: Ss. Felice, sacerdote, e Adautto, martiri, sulla via Ostiense
summary: Felix was a priest taken to execution. Tradition says another Christian joined him on the way and shared his martyrdom as Adauctus.

sourceHeading: San Raimundo Nonnato, cardinale, sacerdote mercedario
summary: Raymond Nonnatus joined the Mercedarians and travelled to North Africa. He endured imprisonment before returning to Spain.
Giles lived as a hermit in southern France. He later became an abbot and a spiritual guide for the surrounding region.
Boniface I became pope after a disputed election in 418. His pontificate worked to restore stability in the Church of Rome.
Marinus was a stonemason from Dalmatia who withdrew to Mount Titano. Tradition connects his Christian community with the origins of San Marino.
God called Moses to lead Israel out of slavery. Through him, the people received the Law and journeyed toward the promised land.
Onesiphorus supported Paul during his imprisonment in Rome. The letter to Timothy remembers his faithful and generous service.
Regina was a young Christian from Alise in Gaul. Tradition remembers her martyrdom after she refused to abandon her faith.
Pope Sergius I came from a Syrian family in Sicily. He sought peace while resisting imperial pressure over Church teaching and practice.
Thomas of Villanova served as Archbishop of Valencia. He cared especially for poor and young people and supported the formation of priests.
Gorgonius was an early Roman martyr buried on the Via Labicana. His tomb drew devotion from Christians over many centuries.
Audomar, also called Omer, became Bishop of Therouanne. He worked to renew the Christian faith in the surrounding region.

sourceHeading: Beato Bonaventura da Barcellona, religioso francescano
summary: Bonaventure of Barcelona performed humble tasks as a Franciscan brother. He established retreats to renew the order's original life of prayer.
This observance honours Mary's name and her love for Jesus. It invites Christians to turn to the mother of the Redeemer in prayer.
Guy of Anderlecht worked as a sacristan and sought to help poor people. His later pilgrimage took him to Rome and the Holy Land.

sourceHeading: San Nicomede, martire sulla via Nomentana
summary: Nicomedes was a Roman priest who buried persecuted Christians. Tradition remembers his refusal of pagan sacrifice and his martyrdom.
Catherine of Genoa turned from a privileged life to serving poor and sick people. Her work included care for people with serious disease.

sourceHeading: Ss. Cornelio, papa e Cipriano, vescovo, martiri
summary: Pope Cornelius and Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage, defended the faith during persecution. The Church honours their witness together as martyrs.
Euphemia suffered martyrdom at Chalcedon during Diocletian's persecution. The great council of 451 later met in the basilica dedicated to her.
Victor III served for many years as abbot of Montecassino. During his short papacy, he worked to restore a troubled Church.

sourceHeading: Santa Colomba, vergine e martire di Cordova
summary: Columba was a nun near Cordoba who studied Scripture. She publicly professed her Christian faith during persecution and was killed in 853.

sourceHeading: San Giuseppe da Copertino, sacerdote francescano
summary: Joseph of Cupertino was a Franciscan with little formal education. He is remembered for his mystical life and as a patron of students.
Sophia is remembered in the Greek calendar with Irene. Few details survive beyond the tradition of her martyrdom in Cyprus.

sourceHeading: San Gennaro, vescovo di Benevento e martire
summary: Januarius, Bishop of Benevento, suffered martyrdom during Diocletian's persecution. He is honoured as the patron of Naples.
Pamphilus was an early Christian martyr buried along Rome's old Via Salaria. Pilgrims were honouring his memory by the seventh century.
Tradition associates Ephigenia with the spread of Christianity in Ethiopia. It remembers her conversion through the Apostle Matthew.
Emerita was a Roman martyr buried in the cemetery of Commodilla. Her relics were later brought to San Marcello al Corso.
Linus succeeded Peter as Bishop of Rome. The Church remembers his ministry among the earliest leaders of the Roman Christian community.
Columba Gabriel was a Polish Benedictine abbess who later served poor people in Rome. She founded the Benedictine Sisters of Charity to help working women.

sourceHeading: San Firmino, vescovo di Amiens e martire
summary: Firmin came from Pamplona and preached in Gaul. As Bishop of Amiens, he refused to renounce his faith and suffered martyrdom.
Cosmas and Damian were Christian brothers who practised medicine without payment. They suffered martyrdom and are honoured as patrons of medical workers.
Little is known about Senator, an early Christian martyr. His memory is associated with a church at Albano Laziale on the Via Appia.

sourceHeading: San Vincenzo de’ Paoli, sacerdote, fondatore della Congregazione della Missione e delle Figlie della Carità, patrono di tutte le Associazioni di Carità
summary: Vincent de Paul devoted his priesthood to practical charity. He founded communities to serve people in need and worked to improve priestly formation.

sourceHeading: Santi Adolfo e Giovanni, martiri a Cordova
summary: Adolph and John were brothers from Seville who professed Christianity in Cordoba. They suffered martyrdom there during the ninth century.
Eustochium accompanied her mother Paula to the Holy Land. At Bethlehem, she lived a consecrated life and became a skilled student of Hebrew.

sourceHeading: Beato Nicola da Forca Palena, sacerdote gerolamino
summary: Nicholas of Forca Palena was a priest and hermit. He established a religious house dedicated to Onuphrius on Rome's Janiculum Hill.
Gabriel is the archangel who announces God's message. The Church celebrates him with Michael and Raphael and honours him as patron of communications.

sourceHeading: San Girolamo, sacerdote e dottore della Chiesa
summary: Jerome devoted his life to Scripture and translated biblical texts into Latin. His study, writing, and ascetic life served the Church.
Simeon, Count of Crepy, gave up wealth and marriage for monastic life. As a hermit in the Jura, he guided pilgrims seeking wisdom.
Francis Borgia was a husband, father, and viceroy before becoming a Jesuit after his wife's death. He later helped lead the order.
The Church honours guardian angels as messengers sent by God. This observance recalls their unseen care and guidance for people.

sourceHeading: Santa Candida, martire sulla via Portuense
summary: Candida is remembered as an early Roman martyr associated with the Via Portuense. Tradition connects her witness with the burial of another martyr.

sourceHeading: Ss. Placido e Mauro, discepoli di San Benedetto
summary: Placidus and Maurus were disciples of Benedict at Subiaco. A well-known monastic account tells of Maurus rescuing Placidus from drowning.

sourceHeading: San Bruno di Calabria, sacerdote, fondatore dei Certosini
summary: Bruno left a promising Church career to seek solitude. He founded a community at Chartreuse and later returned to hermit life in Calabria.

sourceHeading: Santa Maria Francesca delle cinque piaghe, vergine francescana
summary: Mary Frances of the Five Wounds was a Franciscan tertiary in Naples. She chose consecrated life and offered her many sufferings to God.
Pope Mark served for only a few months in 336. His pontificate is associated with the Roman church dedicated to Mark the Evangelist.
Sergius and Bacchus were soldiers who became Christians. They suffered martyrdom in Syria and have long been honoured together.

sourceHeading: Santa Pelagia, vergine e martire di Antiochia
summary: Pelagia is remembered as a Christian woman of Antioch. The Vatican account notes differing traditions about her life.

sourceHeading: Ss. Dionigi, vescovo, e compagni, martiri di Parigi
summary: Denis was an early Bishop of Paris who preached in Gaul. He and his companions Rusticus and Eleutherius are honoured as martyrs.

sourceHeading: San Giovanni Leonardi, fondatore dei Chierici Regolari della Madre di Dio
summary: John Leonardi became a priest after first training as an apothecary. He founded the Clerics Regular of the Mother of God and promoted religious teaching.
Abraham followed God's call with Sarah and his household. His trust in God made him a central figure in the faith of Israel.

sourceHeading: San Paolino, vescovo di York, discepolo di San Gregorio Magno
summary: Paulinus was a monk sent by Gregory the Great to preach in Britain. As Bishop of York, he helped bring rulers and communities to Christianity.

sourceHeading: Santi Daniele, Samuele e Compagni, primi martiri francescani
summary: Daniel, Samuel, and five Franciscan companions preached in Morocco. They refused to renounce their faith and suffered martyrdom at Ceuta in 1227.
Philip was one of the seven chosen to serve the early Church. He preached in Samaria and later welcomed Paul at Caesarea.
Alexander Sauli joined the Barnabites and became their leader. As a bishop, he cared for both the spiritual and material needs of his people.
Pope John XXIII brought long diplomatic and pastoral experience to his office. He called the Second Vatican Council to address the needs of the time.
Edistus is an early martyr whose story survives mainly in legend. Tradition connects his conversion with a Christian community near Rome.
Seraphin of Montegranaro was a humble Capuchin brother. He offered comfort through his devotion to the crucifix and the Rosary.
Theophilus became Christian through reading Scripture and observing Christian life. As Bishop of Antioch, he wrote to explain and defend the faith.

sourceHeading: San Callisto I, papa e martire
summary: Callistus endured slavery and exile before serving the Church in Rome. As pope, he defended the faith and supported mercy toward sinners.

sourceHeading: Santa Margherita Maria Alacoque, vergine, della Visitazione
summary: Margaret Mary Alacoque was a Visitation nun in Burgundy. Her reported visions helped spread devotion to the Sacred Heart of Jesus.
Gerard Majella became a Redemptorist brother after earlier rejection by another community. He performed humble work and bore false accusations with patience.
Peter Casani joined Joseph Calasanz in the Piarists. He shared the conviction that education could guide young people toward salvation.

sourceHeading: San Paolo della Croce, sacerdote, fondatore dei Passionisti
summary: Paul of the Cross founded the Passionists. His community centred its prayer and preaching on Christ's Passion as an expression of divine love.

sourceHeading: Santa Maria Bertilla Boscardin, vergine, di Vicenza
summary: Maria Bertilla Boscardin served as a nurse in Treviso. She continued her religious vocation through serious illness and died at thirty-four.

sourceHeading: San Gaspare del Bufalo, sacerdote, fondatore dei Missionari del Preziosissimo Sangue
summary: Gaspar del Bufalo preached among poor and neglected communities. He founded the Missionaries of the Precious Blood to renew Christian life.
Hilarion became Christian while studying in Alexandria. Inspired by Anthony, he embraced solitude and helped establish monastic communities in Palestine.
Mark became Bishop of Jerusalem in the second century. He worked to rebuild a Christian community weakened by persecution.

sourceHeading: San Giovanni da Capestrano, sacerdote francescano, patrono dei cappellani militari
summary: John of Capistrano became a Franciscan after experiencing imprisonment. He preached widely in Europe and is honoured as patron of military chaplains.

sourceHeading: San Severino Boezio, filosofo romano e martire
summary: Boethius was a Roman philosopher who wrote The Consolation of Philosophy during imprisonment. His work connected classical thought with the developing Christian intellectual tradition.

sourceHeading: Sant'Antonio Maria Claret, vescovo, fondatore della Congregazione dei Figli del Cuore Immacolato di Maria
summary: Anthony Mary Claret founded the Missionary Sons of the Immaculate Heart of Mary. He later continued his missionary calling as a bishop in Cuba.
Crispin and Crispinian worked as shoemakers at Soissons. They shared their Christian faith and suffered martyrdom during persecution.

sourceHeading: Ss. Crisanto e Daria, martiri, sulla via Salaria nuova
summary: Chrysanthus became Christian while studying in Rome. Tradition remembers Daria's conversion through him and their shared martyrdom.
Demetrius is widely honoured as a martyr, especially at Thessalonica. Few historical details of his life are certain.
Evaristus was one of the early successors of Peter as Bishop of Rome. Little is known about his pontificate.
Frumentius reached Ethiopia while enslaved. After gaining freedom and becoming a bishop, he helped the Christian community at Axum grow.
Felician is remembered as a Christian martyr of Carthage. Few details of his life survive beyond his witness to the faith.
Germanus gave his wealth to poor people before becoming Bishop of Capua. His mission to Constantinople helped restore communion between East and West.
Alphonsus Rodriguez entered the Jesuits after losing his wife and children. As a porter in Mallorca, he became known for humble and faithful service.

sourceHeading: Santa Silvia, madre di San Gregorio Magno
summary: Sylvia raised Gregory the Great in a Christian household. She later withdrew to a life of prayer near Saint Paul Outside the Walls.

sourceHeading: Santi Vitale e Agricola, martiri bolognesi
summary: Agricola and his servant Vitalis were Christians in Bologna. Both endured persecution and accepted martyrdom rather than abandon their faith.

sourceHeading: San Villibrordo, vescovo nell'Europa del Nord
summary: Willibrord left England to preach in northern Europe. As Bishop of Utrecht, he continued missionary journeys and later died at Echternach.
Pope Adeodatus I, also called Deusdedit, served from 615 to 618. His short pontificate fell in a period of doctrinal conflict and hardship.
Theodore was a Christian soldier stationed at Amasea. He rejected pagan worship and suffered martyrdom for his faith.
Andrew Avellino became a priest and joined the Theatines in Naples. He died while celebrating Mass in 1608.
Bartholomew helped Nilus establish Grottaferrata. The Byzantine monk cared for poor people and wrote hymns and an account of Nilus's life.
Agostina Pietrantoni was a Sister of Charity who nursed patients in Rome. A patient killed her at Santo Spirito Hospital in 1894.

sourceHeading: Sant'Alberto Magno, vescovo e dottore della Chiesa, domenicano
summary: Albert the Great was a Dominican teacher and theologian. He taught Thomas Aquinas and balanced scholarship with many responsibilities in the Church.
Joseph Pignatelli remained faithful to his Jesuit vocation through expulsion and hardship. He worked for the restoration of the Society of Jesus.
Margaret of Scotland joined family and royal duties with charity. She supported her husband Malcolm III and helped renew the Scottish Church.
Gertrude grew up at Helfta and devoted her life to Christ. Her mystical experiences and writings became part of the Church's spiritual heritage.

sourceHeading: S. Agnese di Assisi, sorella di S. Chiara, vergine
summary: Agnes followed her sister Clare into religious life at San Damiano. She helped establish another Poor Clare community in Florence.
Rose Philippine Duchesne's early religious plans were interrupted by the French Revolution. She later became a missionary in the United States.
Romanus was a deacon who urged Christians to remain faithful during persecution. He was arrested and suffered martyrdom for his witness.
Odo became a monk at Cluny after preparing for a different career. He helped renew monastic life through faithful observance of Benedict's rule.
Obadiah is one of the minor prophets. His short biblical book condemns Edom's conduct and proclaims God's judgment.

sourceHeading: San Clemente I, papa e martire
summary: Clement of Rome was an early pope and Apostolic Father. His letter to the Corinthians urged peace and order within their community.
Tradition remembers Felicity as a Christian widow who encouraged her seven sons during persecution. She shared their martyrdom and was buried in Rome.
Chrysogonus suffered martyrdom at Aquileia during Diocletian's persecution. Devotion to him spread widely in the early Church.
Moses was a Roman priest who showed mercy toward Christians who had denied their faith. He died after a long imprisonment in 251.

sourceHeading: San Pietro d'Alessandria, vescovo e martire
summary: Peter, Bishop of Alexandria, led his Church through persecution and division. He was imprisoned and killed in 311.

sourceHeading: San Leonardo da Porto Maurizio, francescano
summary: Leonard of Port Maurice was a Franciscan preacher who called people to repentance. He promoted the Stations of the Cross, including at Rome's Colosseum.

sourceHeading: San Silvestro, abate, fondatore dei Silvestrini
summary: Sylvester first lived as a hermit in the mountains of central Italy. He later gathered a community following Benedict's rule, known as the Sylvestrines.
Virgilius was an Irish monk who became Bishop of Salzburg. He worked to spread the faith and establish peace in Bavaria.
Nahum was one of Israel's minor prophets. His book presents the fall of Nineveh as God's judgment against evil.
Bibiana's life is known through tradition rather than confirmed history. Her story remembers a young woman who resisted pressure to abandon Christ.

sourceHeading: San Pimenio, martire sulla via Portuense
summary: Pimenius was a priest and teacher in Rome. Tradition remembers his care for martyrs' burial and his own martyrdom.
Pope Silverius was deposed and forced to resign during a Church conflict. He died in exile on the island of Palmarola.
Tradition remembers Barbara as a young woman who remained Christian despite her father's opposition. She suffered martyrdom and is honoured as patron of firefighters.
Sabas left home to become a monk. He established a monastic community in Palestine and defended the Church's teaching about Christ.
Asella lived a consecrated life in fourth-century Rome. She combined prayer and fasting with care for poor people and devotion to the martyrs.

sourceHeading: Sant'Eutichiano, papa, nel cimitero di Calisto
summary: Pope Eutychian served in the third century. His pontificate is remembered for opposing Manichaean teaching and honouring the martyrs.
Leocadia was a young Christian from Toledo. She was arrested during Diocletian's persecution and died in prison.
Syrus was the first Bishop of Pavia. His travelling ministry helped spread Christianity across a wide area of northern Italy.
Peter Fourier was a canon regular and parish priest in Lorraine. He opposed exploitative lending and founded free schools for children.
Our Lady of Loreto is associated with the shrine of the Holy House. Generations of pilgrims have prayed there in honour of Mary.

sourceHeading: San Mauro, martire sulla via Salaria
summary: Maurus was a young martyr remembered at a cemetery on the Via Salaria. Pope Damasus praised his steadfast faith under suffering.
Pope Gregory III came from Syria and served from 731 to 741. He defended sacred images and supported the Church's growth in Germany.
Pope Damasus I preserved the memory of martyrs through inscriptions at their tombs. He also commissioned work on a Latin translation of Scripture.
Pope Gregory III came from Syria and served from 731 to 741. He defended sacred images and supported the Church's growth in Germany.
Little is known about the early martyr Ariston. A church on the Via Ostiense honoured him with Christina and Victoria by the seventh century.
Hyacinthe Cormier was a Dominican known for deep faith and clear teaching. Despite poor health as a novice, he lived to help renew his order.

sourceHeading: Beata Maria degli Apostoli, fondatrice delle Suore Salvatoriane
summary: Mary of the Apostles, born Therese von Wullenweber, sought a missionary vocation. After meeting John Baptist Jordan, she founded the Salvatorian Sisters.
Melania the Younger and her husband Pinian moved to Jerusalem. She gave her wealth to poor people and established a monastic community.
Dismas is the traditional name of the repentant thief crucified beside Jesus. He turned to Christ at Calvary and received the promise of paradise.
Dymphna is remembered as an Irish woman who cared for people with mental illness at Geel. Her legacy inspired centuries of welcome and community care.
Mark and Marcellian were Roman Christians who refused to abandon their faith after arrest. They suffered martyrdom and were buried along the Via Ardeatina.
sourceHeading: Santi Marco e Marcelliano, martiri romani

summary: Zachary and Elizabeth were the parents of John the Baptist. The Vatican News calendar remembers them together.
Tradition remembers Hermes as a Greek man who became Christian in Rome with his household. He was arrested and suffered martyrdom.
Alfred Ildefons Schuster was a Benedictine who became Archbishop of Milan and a cardinal. He remained close to his people through the hardship of war.
sourceHeading: Beato Alfredo Ildefonso Schuster, cardinale, arcivescovo di Milano

summary: Our Lady of Sorrows recalls Mary standing beside the Cross of Jesus. Her faithful presence offers an example of obedience and compassion in suffering.
Hildegard of Bingen was a Benedictine abbess, writer, and composer. Her prayer, teaching, and care for her communities helped renew Christian life.
Basilla is remembered as a martyr during the persecution of Diocletian and Maximian. She was buried along the old Via Salaria.
The Mercedarian tradition honours Mary as Mother of Mercy. Her faith and obedience inspire service to people suffering from captivity, poverty, and violence.
